subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, February 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-93, an act to implement certain government organization provisions of the budget tabled in the House on February 25, 1992, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Economics envelope.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, like most of my colleagues, I would also like to comment on this bill, which concerns the implementation of certain government organization provisions of the budget tabled in the House of Commons on February 25, 1992.
The budget tabled by the minister on February 25, 1992, was an unsuccessful attempt to streamline federal government operations. In 1984 the Conservative government tried to convince us it could control public spending, reduce the deficit and reduce the debt. Today, eight years and several months after an economic recovery that is unique in this country's history, followed by 33 tax increases, we are now back where we were and even worse, because today the debt has at least doubled and the deficit is about the same as it was in 1984.
In February 1992 the Minister of Finance tried to reduce the deficit by restructuring a number of government organizations and agencies. We know from past experience that every time the government tries to reduce the deficit by making cutbacks, the opposite happens. That is why I find it hard to accept this plan to
restructure agencies that have done good work and are in fact badly needed at this time. To cope with globalization, we need the advice of our scientists and economists, and we have to prepare our human resources for the fierce world competition they will have to face.
Unfortunately, in his budget the minister proposes to wind up a number of organizations, including the Petroleum Monitoring Agency, the Pay Research Bureau, the Law Reform Commission, the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security and the Economic Council of Canada. This is unacceptable. The government also wants to close the Science Council of Canada and the Demographic Review Secretariat.
This government always seems to pick the wrong time to do things. It introduced the GST at the worst possible moment in our history, when we were getting into a terrible economic recession. The same thing happened with free trade with the United States. Now it wants us to enter into a free trade agreement with the United States and Mexico. This is one more example of bad timing.
On Sunday, there will be a big demonstration in Montreal to protest the unemployment insurance reforms proposed by this government. Today, we heard there are more than a million and a half unemployed workers in this country and now the government wants to make things even worse for these people. People who still have a job have something else to worry about, because if they lose their job, they might not receive unemployment insurance benefits. We saw a few examples yesterday in the media, where employers have already started to tighten the screws on their employees in anticipation of the new legislation. You can imagine the mental anguish of these people.
I would not say the government does it on purpose, but lately I have been trying to understand why, when they introduce new measures, they always pick the worst possible time. The government has plenty of advisers: it has thousands of public servants. I really fail tounders-tand why this government always tries to make life more difficult for Canadians because that is what it is doing.


Government Orders
What it forgets among all the structures and systems it is trying to implement is that behind all that, the first consideration is a human being, someone with a human face. In everything we do and that must be done, we must always remember that we are dealing with people first and foremost. Every time we introduce a new measure in this House as an opposition member, a government member or a minister and every time we do something in a parliamentary committee or in caucus, that measure affects people. We should think of those affected first. Unfortunately we can see that in the past eight years we have forgotten the human element.
I come back to unemployment insurance. For those who leave their job voluntarily, let us say without just cause, the law already provided a penalty, a waiting period of one to six weeks. In 1990 the government decided to extend this penalty, this waiting period, and made it seven to twelve weeks. So someone who quit without just cause would be penalized for three months and I wonder who would deliberately leave a job to stay at home and receive nothing for three months. Is that really credible? This morning, I learned that another major Quebec institution opposed to this bill, the Legal Commission, says that this kind of abuse that the government wants to avoid or get rid of is almost non-existent; there is none. That is not the problem with our unemployment insurance system.
So again it is introducing a measure that does not correspond to reality, that does not solve our problems but creates more victims and places other people in a bad situation.

The Prime Minister is in Washington today. One of the slogans of the President of the United States in the last election was putting people first. I hope while he is in Washington the Prime Minister thinks seriously about that phrase putting people first because everything we do in this place, everything we say, whether in this House, in cabinet, in our communities or in our caucuses, affects people.
We are here to help people. We are not here to help big business; they have all the help they need. They have
consultants, lawyers, accountants, lobbyists, whatever they want.
The people who really need unemployment insurance want to know it is there for them. However, that the law does not provide. Before, if they had to quit their jobs, they could count on unemployment insurance. As we saw in the December 2 budget and in the bill before the House, conditions are now applied, otherwise there is no unemployment insurance.
What are these people going to do? Those who qualify will go on social welfare, but many do not qualify. Some in my riding who lost their jobs more than a year ago have no unemployment insurance and they do not qualify for social welfare because they own a house. They worked so hard to buy a home and now there is no UI, no job, and they will have to sell their homes if they want to eat. That is the point we are at and Bill C-105 does not help the situation.
It makes it worse for some people who have jobs. If something happens that they have to leave their jobs, perhaps they do not get along with the employer, they will be in that situation as well.
We are not doing our job because we are not helping people. We are not putting people first.

Madam Speaker, you are indicating to me that my time is up. I would still have a lot more to say, but I hope that in this difficult period my colleagues on the government side will be able to put pressure on their ministers and that in making their decisions they will think of people first.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to speak on this bill this morning. In some ways I am delighted to do so because it gives me an opportunity to express my views, and the views of my party, which are very much in line with my hon. colleague from Saint-Leonard.
Frequently in speaking on these issues there is difficulty trying to follow the pattern of the government with its arrogance and insensitivity in pursuing its economicpoli-cies, particularly as they pertain to eastern Canada and particularly as they pertain to the maritimes.


The purpose of Bill C-93 is to implement certain changes made by the budget tabled in February of last year. The bill is divided into 10 parts and rather than speak on each of the parts, I want to restrict my comments to the Atlantic Canada Opportunity Agency and particularly the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation which the government is proposing be closed down.
I want to put this in the perspective of where we are sitting on this side of the House and the kinds of things I have heard in the last four and a half years. In the case of my colleagues to my immediate left, some of them have been listening a lot more than eight years to the economic policies of the Conservative government.
When I was campaigning during the election before I came to this House, I recall the general promises that were made in philosophical terms. As the country is now struggling out of a recession, the Conservative government member, in preparing for an election, will be going back and asking Canadians to elect them at a time when they have failed miserably in the essential elements of their four-pillar policy. I am going to quote it because I think this has to be done in the backdrop of this policy. They talked about economic reform, social justice, national reconciliation and constructive internationalism.
They asked people, either philosophically or specifically, to put aside their personal concerns and make further sacrifices in the name of global competitiveness and long-term prosperity. As I speak today, the kind of prosperity I see around me in Newfoundland and in Atlantic Canada, in the western part of Canada, and indeed in all of Canada, is jobless prosperity.
My colleague from Toronto tells me the difficulty that one has. My colleagues from the west tell me the difficulty that we have. I do not have to speak to anybody to tell of the difficulty we have in Newfoundland. I am sure I speak for my colleagues from Nova Scotia and particularly from Cape Breton, and I know that part of the country very well, when I tell you the difficulties that they are having there which are not unlike those difficulties we are having in Newfoundland and that were epitomized and highlighted to such a pathetic degree in the last couple of days by the unconscionable action that is being taken in Port Hawkesbury. There was the fly-by-night closure of a plant by a person who got grants from this government and is now getting out of business
Government Orders
and leaving 79 people dismayed, out of work and very angry.
There are a lot of angry people in Atlantic Canada. I think there is a very good reason for it. Having made the promises of the four pillars that I just spoke about on October 3, 1988, the Prime Minister told the Saint John Board of Trade: "We will not have one Canada that is prospering at the centre while the other regions do not receive their fair share of the economic opportunities".
That was in October, 1989. Shortly after that, both the west and Atlantic Canada watched in dismay as in the April budget western diversification was cut drastically and ACOA was essentially cut by 25 per cent. The term used, and I remember it so well, was reprofiling. Reprofiling to ACOA meant a reduction of 25 per cent.
Not only that, but we saw a reduction in regional development and forestry agreements. Military bases were closed, ports were closed, post offices were closed, VIA Rail service was vastly reduced, and it is almost disappearing right now, freight rates were altered and UI regulations were changed to the detriment of most. It includes certainly all fishermen and seasonally employed individuals.
I talked in generalities there. So much for all parts of the country being treated equally. Let me just talk about transfer payments that have happened since 1989 to this very day.
With the implementation of Bill C-20, by the year 2000 the federal government will have essentially kept back from Canadians, according to the best figure I can get, $97.6 billion worth of services and resources that are essentially provided in health care and post-secondary institutions. Federal transfer payments, I would remind hon. members, account for, in a rough order of magnitude, 50 per cent. It used to be. It has now been reduced from 49 per cent to 45 per cent.
With regard to the federal government transfer to Newfoundland, let me put it in a term that can be understood very clearly. From the time I arrived in this House until this very day, the cost to Newfoundlanders, because they had to pick up the tab, in the transfer payment reduction by various bills has worked out to very close to $200 million. When you are dealing with a budget that is in the $3 billion plus range, $200 million isa lot of money and Newfoundlanders are hurting because of it.

Government Orders
I could speak of other examples; the deficit, the goods and services tax being introduced as a bad tax at the wrong time. I could talk about the closing of post offices that are inequitable in various parts of the country. I could talk about any number of things and it would not be a happy message. Let me talk more directly to this particular aspect.
The idea in one of the 10 parts of this bill is to close down Enterprise Cape Breton and move its function and staff to the main office of ACOA.
We are opposed to this move to kill Enterprise Cape Breton for a number of reasons. In the budget speech the government stated that this, along with some of the other organizations, were being eliminated because they had served their purpose and were no longer needed. Nothing can be further from the truth. Enterprise Cape Breton is probably needed more now than it was before.
As I said at the outset of my presentation, the Cape Breton economy is still extremely troubled, as epitomized by the example of Port Hawkesbury. Special programs to address it are certainly needed more than ever but we do not see any programs coming around the comer.
The unemployment rate in Cape Breton right now has reached 25 per cent and is certainly climbing. The rate was only 16 per cent when the corporation was created. Now all of Atlantic Canada, but particularly Cape Breton's economy, faces great challenges today. I would suggest that it faces more challenges today than it did when the corporation was created in 1985.
Why is that? It is just because of the general state of the economy that all Canadians are suffering, or because the unemployment rate is high in all of Canada and is much higher of course in Cape Breton, but because of other factors that have occurred since then.
The business of Cape Breton apart from coal is very much in the fishing business. I am familiar with that and I do not have to tell anybody on any side of the House of the difficulty that fishing has suffered in my riding, which has been closed for the last year, will be for the next year and God knows for how long. It is a very dismal and grim situation.
In Cape Breton the NAFO zones surrounding the Cape Breton littoral have been vastly reduced and now we are in the business of actually reducing the number of licences that bona fide fishermen held through some fluke of the way the catch is organized and the way the catches are credited to the licences. It has not hit my riding yet because very few people are fishing but in the rest of Atlantic Canada and Cape Breton this is a major source of concern.
I believe we have a major problem on our hands. Essentially those who suggest that voters' expectations have become unreasonable or that they are asking for more is a myth. In this particular case, the closing of the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation is not in the interest of Cape Breton and I would suggest it is not in the interest of Canada.
It is not Canada or the political system that is at fault here. In fact it is the government and its policies that are found wanting.

speechtext: The absurdity is that they promised more. They promised more and more and yet their leader has said that fiscal responsibility and restraint, remarkably, has become one of his number one priorities.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It was yours for the last eight and a half years and you have not done anything about it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
If the Liberal Party, the people opposite, are serious about restraint and fiscally responsible government, they should be encouraging the moves that we have made.
The member talks about regional disparities and how we are being unfair to the regions. In my lifetime in Canada, which is now approaching 58 years, I have never seen a Canadian government that has been as fair to the regions. I come from the opposite end of the country from the member. I come from British Columbia. In spite of the restraint that has been required by this government, the fairness we are seeing has never been seen before.


The premier of Alberta was in town just two days ago attesting to the fact that this current Conservative government is finally giving some fairness to the people of Alberta. The prairies are having terribly hard times but we have never seen a Canadian government that has been prepared to try to help as much as this government has.
We all know that the province the previous speaker comes from is suffering terrible hardships but we also know that this government is doing everything it can to be of assistance.
The Hibernia project is not there to take away jobs or wealth from the regions but to provide wealth and provide jobs. The members of our party from central Canada are frantically trying to find solutions for the people in those parts of the country that are suffering the most.
The measures contained in Bill C-93 are part of this government's program of fiscal restraint. Streamlining government will not only save money but it will also increase the efficiency of government and the services it provides to Canadians.
The Liberal leader recently said that deficit control is essential and that fiscal restraint should be and would be one of his number one priorities. However, we have seen the people opposite again and again block, vote against, and do everything they can to prevent any of these fiscally responsible moves which the government is taking.
It is time for the people opposite to match their rhetoric with action. It is time for the Liberals in particular to stop their obstructionist and filibustering tactics and allow Canadians the benefits of fiscally responsible government. Therefore, I move:
That the question be now put.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have three questions, which I will answer. They are: Why is the government proceeding this way? What hashappened since the government made its decision? Finally, have there been proposals from some agencies,
Government Orders
advice or recommendations to the government that could help it if it wanted to look at them carefully and responsibly?

Why is this being done? There have been suggestions that it might be because the government wants to realize savings but it has backed off a bit because we have said: "You put the figures on the table and we will look at them. Let us see how much money is really being saved".
Then it attacked it from another angle, efficiency. Then of course we said: "All right. If you say it is going to be more efficient then show us how it is going to be more efficient". That has not been done and I think that is really quite unfair. Let us look at the real reason. We know that there were a number of those organizations that were no longer functioning and had not operated for a number of years. We know that there were minimal savings in some particular cases.
I will give governments the benefit of the doubt on the questions of savings and efficiency but I want some proof before I can say: "Yes, you are right". Until I get that proof I am not going to accept it.
Let us examine what is probably the real reason. We know there are a lot of people out there who say, with some justification, that there is too much government and that it is too costly. What has the government done? It has taken these organizations and tried to give the impression that it has done something rather large and significant.
My colleague is nodding his head and saying yes. I know he agrees with me.

It is as if the government were trying to give the impression that it was doing something very important, but that is not the case at all. It was to respond to a certain constituency in which it wants to be re-elected.

It has lost a certain number of supporters and it is trying to get them back. Let us be very, very frank. That is why this decision has been made.


Government Orders
The second question is: What has happened since this decision was made? I do not want to talk about each organization, I want to focus on one, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, which is being folded into the Canada Council.
We all know it has been operating since 1977-78 and has been doing very well. We also know that it was set up because there was a vision at that time that Canada's major challenges were social problems. Economic development is a social issue. What about the 1.6 million unemployed and the almost five million who are living either at the level of poverty or below the level of poverty? Most of them are women and over one million of whom are children. What about the 2.3 million Canadians who receive social assistance? What about the more than two million Canadians who will be fed at food banks this year?
We often talk about abuse in our society. This is a social issue that social scientists can study. They can give us precious and valuable advice so that we can find solutions that are meaningful, creative and put our country in the forefront of nations.
Since this government's decision we have received literally hundreds of letters, as many petitions if not more, and roughly the same number of calls. A number of important meetings were held where people have asked us to please make the government understand that the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council is not better off folded into the Canada Council. Please make the government understand that its major challenges today are social issues such as unemployment, abuse, food banks and aid to various people. Please make the government understand that this is a step backward, not a step forward. This is what these people have said in their petitions, their letters, their telephone calls and in the meetings which they have had with me and many other colleagues.
People want the government to understand there will be virtually no savings and no additional efficiency. The fact is that there may be no savings whatsoever. No one sees any efficiency here.
I challenge the government. The government thinks it is right and it has had a number of speakers who have made that point. I ask the Conservatives to find one credible man or woman who has laboured long and hardin the social sciences to stand up and say that what
they are doing here, the folding in of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council into the Canada Council, is a progressive step. I challenge them to find one Canadian, one man or woman who has credibility in the social sciences to say that this is a step forward. If they can, I would be really quite shocked and surprised because I do not think they could find one person. If they can, I am quite willing to acknowledge that, but they will not find him or her and that speaks loudly of this government's decision.
These organizations that have written, sent in petitions, made phone calls and have had meetings have put forward proposals to government. A number of organizations have told us, with some justification, not to do it. It has been working since 1977-78 and we have been making some progress in attacking those social issues and finding creative and meaningful solutions for Canadians. Do not take a step backward. That was one group of people.
When these organizations felt that the government would probably not want to review its decision in spite of the evidence that they had put forward that it was not a good decision, what did they say? They said that they had not been consulted. The government could stop this part and defer it until Canadians have been consulted thoroughly. Subsequent to that study and consultation, if the government feels it is a good decision for Canadians, that it is going to help us resolve much more significantly than we have in the past our social problems, then and only then make the decision.
There has been another group that felt that the government would not even do that.
That is, let them consult Canadians and try to find out if it was really a sound decision. So they proposed something else. They said, "If you cannot stop this bill, if you do not want to consult, we will propose some amendments."

I would ask the government to check very carefully the amendments that have been proposed. I have proposed some. I would be the first to suggest that there may besome that are useful. There may be others that are less useful.


We have amendments from the Social Science Federation of Canada. I saw one set of amendments coming from a group representing 15,000 social scientists in this nation. We have amendments from major national organizations, AUCC, CAUT and others. I would ask the government at the very least to examine those amendments before ramming this bill through. It is the least that it can do.

I will close by saying this. I understand that the government wants to make some changes. I believe that it is quite natural for a government to want to make certain changes, but I would really like it to say honestly that it is making these changes because it wants to try to recover its losses in recent months and years. It is not a matter of efficiency, of streamlining or saving money; it is really to win back some of its lost followers.

That is what I would like the government to do, to put forward its agenda in a truthful, honest way. It is to attract those people it has lost. It has very little to do with anything else, with savings or efficiency. There are a number of proposals on the table. At the very least it should stop this part of the bill and consult Canadians. Then and only then should it decide whether or not this is the best way to proceed to ensure that our social scientists have the tools and the infrastructure in place necessary to attack our grave social problems.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I believe my colleague from St. Boniface has opened up a very important and very useful line of concern about Bill C-93. I was particularly struck by his description of the serious social problems affecting this country and the need to begin developing serious solutions.
If we ever needed more evidence of that problem, we saw it in the figures that were released this morning dealing with the serious problem of unemployment and joblessness in this country. When we talk about a drop-out rate of 56,000 people who have totally and completely given up any hope of getting a job in this country, have dropped out of the labour market, are no longer even convinced that the chance of finding a job is
Government Orders
there, then they are going to become part of a large, broad subterranean grouping of Canadians who are forgotten, neglected, creating a two-tier society, a split-level country. We are setting in place major structural problems for years and years ahead and there is no will, no interest, no concern about dealing with that problem.
This bill talks about reorganizing government to make it more efficient presumably. Efficiency is not the only criteria. Effectiveness, the ability to achieve serious results in terms of the issues and problems facing Canadians is also a prime responsibility of any government.
The tragedy we see today is figures that talk about the continuing sorrow of young Canadians, where the unemployment rate is close to 20 per cent of people under the age of 20. That is becoming a permanent, continuing fact of life in Canada. It is not temporary, not transitory, but one that is becoming part and parcel of the Canadian scene. We have a government that is indifferent to that plight. It refuses to take any action.
It is so ironic that today the Prime Minister is visiting the new President of the United States, saying we have to start on a new foot. We have to get new beginnings and we have to begin establishing new frameworks. The irony is that just two days ago, that new President announced a stimulative program to inject into the economy of the United States $31 billion, which is a much stronger economy than ours. The program will create jobs in infrastructure, public works and deal with the problems of structural unemployment in the cities. These are the very same problems that my colleague from St. Boniface talked about.
Our Prime Minister and our Minister of Finance reject any opportunity to co-operate with the Americans to develop a stimulative economic package that would help us develop a response to give some hope back to those
66,000	people who dropped out of the work force today.
We can only hope and pray that perhaps on the way to Washington, like Saul on the road to Tarsus, the Prime Minister will have a revelation and will come back with some understanding that this economy needs a stimulus, that young people need hope, that Canadians need jobsand that we have to come to grips with a kind of underlying burden of unemployment in this country.


Government Orders
Perhaps the new President of the United States can use his persuasive powers to convince and overcome the stubbornness of our present administration. It is time for a change. It is time for a change in direction to deal with this serious problem.
I want to point out one other aspect of this bill that again is tinged with enormous irony. We are talking about a need to reorganize, presumably to make things work more effectively.
One of the aspects of this bill which will not demand headlines but certainly concerns me is how it will affect Canada's representation abroad. It has become a cliche to say we live in a global economy. What is important about that fact of life is that so much of our trade, our relations, depends on how Canadians are perceived.
In a recent Angus Reid poll, taken in 15 other countries, unfortunately the prominent perception of people abroad is that the Canadians are far too dependent on the foreign policy of our southern neighbour.
We have to try and change perceptions and realizations. One way is to ensure that there is an effective understanding of the culture and education of this country. We have tried, even though it has been poorly financed and not properly supported, through the external affairs department, to set up Canadian studies programs in countries around the world, where in universities, high schools and educational institutions there would be a greater understanding of what Canada is all about, our concerns and our issues.
In Bill C-93 that program is being folded into the Canada Council. The program is being eliminated from external affairs which already has the structure abroad to make that case and it is being folded into the Canada Council.
To make some genuflexion in that direction, the amendment to the Canada Council Act reads:
In performing its international functions and duties, the council
should take into account the foreign policy of the Government of
Canada.
To begin with, there is a fundamental problem. We have to discern what the foreign policy of Canada really is.
More important, why are we creating a duplication of effort in setting up the Canada Council, which will have to establish people to work abroad at the same time as we are eliminating that function in external affairs? Is that what we call an efficient use of resources? Do we take with one hand and set up a new institution with the other?
I can foresee in the days ahead that we will now have Canada Council representatives in various countries abroad, duplicating what the external affairs department was already doing but not being part of an integrated, coherent activity. It will be fragmented and separated, trying to discern what should be the foreign policy of Canada.
It becomes a matter of serious credibility when a government says that these measures are being taken to save money and to get more efficient delivery of services. If we look at what is going to happen, it is duplication of services and the recreation of a function. It adds on to another agency a task that is already being performed. There is simply no rhyme or reason in this proposed reorganization. It simply does not make good common sense.
Surely we are dealing with scarce resources and trying to find out the best way of ensuring that Canadian interests overseas and in the international environment are effectively and properly carried forward. At the same time they are once again disrupting the functioning of an active program, turning it over to another agency, thereby creating a new function, hiring new people, getting them trained and trying to integrate it with what is already taking place.
One has to ask: Where is the common sense in that kind of approach? Again to use the remarks of my colleague from St. Boniface, it totally disrupts the ability in a very important way to come to grips with the understanding of these issues. The social sciences and humanities is the study of people. We must look at how the problems of people have to be dealt with.
It is a different set of intellectual, academic and research concerns than dealing with the arts. A totally different set of judgments has to be made. Different players have to be involved. Yet they are also being folded in without any particular coherence being given for their function.


It is very difficult for us to say that we can support a bill which cripples the ability of this country to come to grips with its economic and social problems, which duplicates its functions abroad and which ends up in my view costing more money, fragmenting our functions and duplicating something that is already being done. That simply does not make good common sense.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to Bill C-93.
I must say at the outset that the bill reminds me of the historical reality-and we can us it as a metaphor-that while the emperor fiddles, Rome bums. In this country we see the government spending a lot of attention fiddling with organizations, small departments, and so on. Perhaps some change is justified, but while attention from the government is focused on these small issues which have great significance and impact on certain people, our country's major issues are not being dealt with.
My colleagues spoke very well about some of those issues, but the biggest problem is that we are forced by this government to pay attention to this bill and what it is that the government is proposing to do. The government has not really rationalized the content of the this bill and told us, explained clearly, or allowed the public to have adequate input into why this bill is good for this country.
As has been mentioned by some of my colleagues, I certainly have great difficulty with the parts of this bill which wind up the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and transfer its function and staff to the Canada Council and, as my colleague before me eloquently stated, transfer certain functions and staff of the Department of External Affairs concerned with the promotion of Canadian culture to the Canada Council.
I have heard many people express deep concern about this move. They have expressed very strongly that this move is not advised. Particularly with the winding down of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council into the Canada Council, it is pitting different groups against each other instead of trying to promote their individual functions, which are very different but very important to the future of our country. Specifically it is those functions which fall in the Social Sciences and Humanities area versus those that are more focused upon Canadian culture. They are two different functions
Government Orders
but both are very important to the future of this country. They are not pitted against each other.
Another colleague spoke very eloquently about the winding down of the Enterprise Cape Breton corporation without having a full review and a full understanding on the part of the Canadian public about the implications. It goes on and on.
A colleague on the other side of the House said this was just another example of a fiscally responsible government. However we are not assured at all, in reviewing and analysing the actions planned by this bill, that what we are doing thereby is going to be more efficient or more economic. Sometimes when we see bills like this one it appears the government is panicking in its desperate desire to find ways to free up money. It does not appear that it is actually accomplishing its stated goal of doing that, but instead, in a panic it is just rushing to cut programs without good rationalization.
In my riding of Northumberland people are suffering grievously from the cuts this government has made to various programs. The whole emphasis of this government for the last eight years has been to cut in the name of debt and deficit reduction. We on this side of the House support that as well, but we simply cannot irrationally cut programs without a good analysis of the consequences of doing so. We are now living with the consequences of this government's irrational cuts.
Besides being very concerned about debt and deficit reduction, we should be equally concerned about increasing wealth and about increasing our Gross Domestic Product so that we can analyse where we are going as a country. Indeed as government we always have to review what programs and policies we are supporting and what the rationalization is.
There are some very good programs in place, specifically our social safety nets. We should not be getting rid of them as we have been. We must maintain national programs of communication which we see being eroded day after day, be it Canadian National Railways, VIA, the post office or the CBC. We see irrational cuts of programs being done to reduce debt, but we have not looked at how we can, instead of cutting, improve those programs, make them more efficient, make them more economic and at the same time put a very strong emphasis on other programs and investments that can bemade by this government to increase the wealth of this country.

One of the main factors of growth are our small businesses. Major employers in this country have been hurt grievously by the cuts of this government. We see so much unemployment and so much misery, and the bottom line is that our municipalities are having to bear the great burden for that, that this party cannot support the in many instances unjustified cuts in this Bill C-93.

Madam Speaker, while this government has made substantive improvements to the Young Offenders Act, I was pleased to learn that this and related legislation is to receive further consideration this year. To help provide greater peace and security for our Canadian homes and families, there are two additional changes I would recommend to the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General.
First, sentencing for repeat offences under the Young Offenders Act should be more meaningful and consistent with the severity of the crimes committed. Second, after conviction, the names of those found guilty should be made public so that people can have a clear understanding of what is going on in their community.
I am sure these changes would be welcomed by my constituents in Durham, and most certainly by a great majority of Canadians.

Madam Speaker, since the adoption of its corporate plan in 1986, Canada Post has shut down over 1,200 post offices under a so-called natural opportunity policy. Under this policy all 5,221 rural post offices are scheduled to be closed down over a 10-year period. Individual post offices are shut down when the natural opportunity
of retirement, resignation or death of a postmaster occurs.
Recently there were six cases of post offices in and around the Prime Minister's riding where the postmasters had retired. Instead of opening the natural opportunity, new postmasters were hired and post offices remained open in five of six cases.
Why is it that a post office serving 121 people is kept open in the Prime Minister's backyard, while those serving thousands of people as in Spaniard's Bay and other Newfoundland communities are being shut down?
The minister responsible for Canada Post says that Canadians favour the closing and privatizing of post offices. If this is the case, why are post offices in the Prime Minister's riding being kept open? It seems there is one rule for the Prime Minister and another for the rest of us.

Madam Speaker, once again I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the decision last February to allow first-time home buyers to purchase a home with a 5 per cent rather than a 10 per cent down payment.
During the first year of this program it has been utilized by 68,806 home buyers. When it was first introduced 12 months ago, the minister estimated that it might help some 20,000 home buyers over the entire two-year lifetime of the program. Yet the combination of lower house prices and stable mortgage rates in most parts of Canada has more than tripled the demand for the 5 per cent down payments in the first year alone.
Obviously the program has been a smashing success, not only because it has directly increased home ownership and indirectly increased the supply of rental accommodation, but also because it has increased consumer spending-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret the hon. member's time has expired.

Madam Speaker, across Canada thousands of grandparents live with the agony of never being able to have contact with their grandchildren. They live with the daily despair of knowing their grandchildren may think that their grandparents no longer love them or want to see them.
David and Madeleine Bremner are two such grandparents. For three years since the tragic death of their young daughter they have not been allowed to visit, write or talk with their grandsons in Nova Scotia. Their cards, letters, Christmas cards, Christmas presents and birthday presents are returned unopened.
Quebec law ensures that the loving bonds between grandparents and grandchildren cannot be broken without cause, yet this government has refused to consider the same measures.
I ask it to please listen to the petitions of despairing grandparents. People who want to support grandparents may request a petition from my office.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today, all of Canada, but especially the people of Quebec, mourn the loss of Frangoys Bernier, this great musician who was carried off by a long illness that he fought bravely until the end.
Frangoys Bernier started his career at Gravelbourg College, in Saskatchewan. Later, he was musical director for the Montreal Festivals, artistic director for the Quebec Symphony Orchestra and Chairman of the Music department at the University of Ottawa.
Frangoys Bernier has put on the Canadian and Quebec charts unique performances that reflected his great talent.
He was a pioneer in interpreting works of Canadian composers, including Roger Matton's Te Deum, when he was the director of the ORTF Orchestra, in Paris.
The crowning achievement of his career was certainly the Domaine Forget of Saint-Irenee, his music school, an establishment located in beautiful Charlevoix which will continue to honour the memory of Frangoys Bernier.
To his family, we extend our deepest sympathies and the assurance that his works and achievements will perpetuate his memory.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to again express concern about the American's use of their anti-dumping provisions to harass Canadian companies. Today it is Canadian farmers whom they are harassing. We have been harassed on softwood, we have been harassed on steel and now we are being harassed on grain.
Yesterday in Question Period I asked the minister of trade a question related to an American expert who talked about the corruption and the harassment that is behind the U.S. anti-dumping laws. I quoted that this reveals the hypocrisy and the absurdity of the U.S. dumping record.
We are being treated as patsies by the American government and by American special interests. It is time for this government to stop allowing the Americans to run railroad rife over all Canadian industries. It is time for this government to stand up for Canadians and say enough is enough.

Madam Speaker, after the last provincial election, the residents of Ontario riding expected a new approach to the serious problem of landfill and garbage disposal in the region of Durham and metro Toronto.
The previous Liberal government had trampled all over the rights of the local residents and was about to impose its wish on the residents of Pickering.

The new NDP government has released its reports and will now consider allowing garbage to be dumped in four locations: in Pickering and in one mega-dump site right on the border of the Rouge Valley watershed. The residents of Pickering and in particular Whitevale deserve better.
I call on the NDP Government of Ontario to open its mind, allow garbage to be dealt with in new ways, investigate new technologies and widen the geographical search for potential landfill sites.

Madam Speaker, yesterday in a legislative committee meeting on Bill C-76 where we were to have examined, among other subjects, the government's imposition of its decision to increase interest on student loans, the government's desire to impose registration fees possibly on the poorest of organizations and the government's changes to the Small Businesses Loans Act, government members refused to allow even one outside witness per clause of the bill.
When the opposition left in protest, government members snuck out, found another Tory robot, a yes person, and rammed the bill through.
Organizations such as the Canadian Federation of Students and the National Anti-Poverty Organization are outraged by the government's contempt for the democratic process and its total disdain for openness and public participation in the political committee process.
Will this government ever learn that it simply cannot treat Canadians unfairly?

Madam Speaker, the NDP has been resorting to their old tactics of scaremongering as they try to frighten Canadians into believing that free trade is bad for Canada.
In fact Bob Rae has hit a new low in using this well-worn tactic. It has been reported recently that at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, politicians from other countries travelled far to boost their countries and their regions but only in Canada did they go abroad to tear down the country. And Bob
Raewonders why the recovery in Ontario is so slow in coming.

Madam Speaker, the Conservative government is continuing to breach the wall of the unemployment insurance plan built to protect the unemployed from the effects of job loss.
The Liberals began to take away the bricks from that wall in 1978 when they reduced benefits by over 6 per cent.
The legislation proposed through Bill C-105 seeks to bring down the wall entirely to establish a level playing field between Canada and the United States. The legislation is a violation of labour standards and human rights. An employer can commit any act of discrimination, order extremes in working conditions, literally get away with almost anything because the results of quitting or firing are total income loss.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to commend the government. It was not many months ago that I was up in this House representing the citizens of Lockport in my riding of Selkirk-Red River.
It was at that time that the status of the Lockport Bridge was in question. The government by way of the Minister of Public Works has responded in spades. The St. Andrews lock and dam and the Lockport Bridge will be refurbished at a cost of $20 million.
This will extend the life of the 82-year old structure well beyond its 100th birthday. On behalf of the citizens of the riding of Selkirk-Red River I thank the government for a quick positive response.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday I brought to the attention of the House how Canada Post has what could best be considered a duplicitous policy on the shutting down ofrural post offices. Today I would like to expand upon that a little bit.


Guess where St-Irenee is? The population, 363, lost its postmaster but kept its post office. Baie St-Paul, population 3,000, still has a post office even though the postmaster retired on March 12, 1992. Forestville still has its post office. St-Simeon, St-Joseph de la Rive. Where are all those places, my colleagues ask? In the riding of Charlevoix.
Who is the MP for that riding?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: The government says it does not interfere with the operations of Canada Post. I would like to ask this government across the way why is it then that the Minister of Public Works was able to get a freeze on the closure of the Westville, Nova Scotia post office?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, tomorrow in Calgary I will be presenting 38 Calgarians with the Queen's commemorative medal marking Canada's 125th birthday. It is indeed fitting that we pay tribute to those citizens who have devoted so much time and energy toward making their country and indeed their communities a better place to live.
Many more Calgarians are equally deserving of recognition and I would like to take this opportunity to extend my sincere gratitude and appreciation to all of them as well. Once again Calgary has proven itself to be truly the city of volunteers and we thank you.

Madam Speaker, in the next few weeks the current Canada-U.S. agreement in respect of cruise missile testing will come to an end. With the Prime Minister meeting today with President Clinton there is an historic opportunity to end cruise missile testing not only in Canada and the United States but around the world. President Yeltsin has made a standing offer to stop cruise missile testing if the Americans will do the same. There are only two coun-triesstill testing cruise missiles, Russia and the United States.
Security in the world depends on using this historic opportunity to negotiate and to bring to an end the arms race while these countries are co-operating. I would call on the government and the Prime Minister to end cruise missile testing now by refusing to renew the Canada-U.S. cruise missile testing agreement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, recent surveys in Calgary Southeast show an increasing alarm in violence against women. A growing number are demanding that we strengthen the laws which protect Canadian women from so-called stalkers and predators.
I am encouraged that the Minister of Justice is taking immediate action. We have the opportunity to demonstrate to Canadians our commitment to protecting women and our families. I urge the minister to press forward with measures designed to combat the terror which faces too many women in our country.

Madam Speaker, according to the Geneva convention any person who has reasonable fears or valid reasons for believing that he or she will be subject to persecution on the basis of their ethnic background, religious belief or political and social activities has the right to seek refugee status. People seek refugee status in Canada precisely because the legal system in their own country of origin has not been able to protect them. The Immigration Refugee Board recently rejected a claim by a young woman from Saudi Arabia who faced deportation on the grounds that she should "respect her father and submit herself to the religious views which govern her country".
Had this woman returned to Saudi Arabia she would have in all certainty been imprisoned or put to death for criticizing Islamic beliefs.
It is obvious that women who are lucky enough to have escaped from lies and total subjugation should qualify as refugees. Rights should be gender blind. I ask theminis-ter to place a moratorium on the deportation of women until new guidelines which incorporate the category of persecution on the basis of sex can be established.

Oral Questions TAXATION

Madam Speaker, while the Liberal Party of Canada ponders a business transfer tax to replace the GST, I ask the Liberal critic for consumer and corporate affairs to publicly raise his objections to a tax that would tax basic groceries, a tax that would tax rent, a tax that would be invisible to consumers, a tax without rebates to low and modest-income Canadians, a tax that governments could raise without consumers knowing and a tax that is ultimately hurtful to consumers.
Where does the Liberal consumer critic stand on his party's very cynical replacement tax for the GST?

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Now that the Prime Minister is meeting his new friend, his best friend, President Clinton, will the Prime Minister emulate Mr. Clinton's policy as reported in The New York Times today and stimulate the Canadian economy? Or does he intend to stay on the same course, with policies that are strangling our economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance delivered a financial statement in December and made many proposals to help the economy of Canada. Today we were pleased to note that the unemployment rate dropped a full one-half percentage point, from 11.5 per cent to 11 per cent.
That is not reason to celebrate wildly by any stretch of the imagination because there are still too many people unemployed in this country, but all the indicators are extremely positive. We have the basics in place and we are expecting a modest but steady recovery in this year 1993. The statistics from the first month of January arevery positive, indicating that we are going to have a good 1993.

Madam Speaker, it is a very sad day when the Government of Canada can congratulate itself on the unemployment of more than a million and a half Canadians.
It is a sad day when there are more than a million children still lining up at food banks.
I want to ask the minister a very direct question. Why is it that this government continues to pursue a stand pat do nothing policy on the economy when our unemployment rate is 11 per cent while in the United States at a 7 per cent unemployment rate President Clinton is prepared to act forcefully? Why does the Prime Minister not take a page from President Clinton's book and stimulate the Canadian economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Liberals one day are knocking the Americans and praising them the next. One of the reasons people of this country will not elect them is because they are all over the map talking about what comes into their minds at that particular moment.
I must say that in the last nine months we have had
161,000	new jobs created in this country. That is very positive. Second, every economic think tank is saying that Canada will lead the G-7 in economic recovery this year. President Clinton has seen that and he does not like to see Canada leading in the G-7. That is why he is doing what he is doing. We made our economic statement back in December, long before President Clinton was even sworn in and we are starting to see some of the results of that economic statement today.

Unfortunately Madam Speaker, Canadians have not gained jobs. What they have done is lost hope.
More than half a million young people in this country cannot get a first job. We have a drop-out rate that should scare every one of us who wants to provide hope to a new generation. The unemployed cannot find work and the government is not even prepared to protect those people with jobs.
With all our problems in the steel industry, will the Prime Minister at least return from Washington with the commitment that U.S. harassment on steel will stop? Can the thousands of Canadian steel workers who are infear of losing their jobs have some comfort about fan-trade between Canada and the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians must be watching the television play of this and saying: "Poor Sheila, just like Bad Luck Schlepprock in the comics, always looking for bad news, always looking for things that can hurt the hope and the confidence that people want to have in the economy today".
Surely, my hon. friend is aware of the 161,000 jobs in the last number of months that are helping people get to work, jobs that are being created by the policies that this government is following.
In specific terms on the steel agreement with the United States, my hon. friend knows this is something that the Prime Minister has already taken to the President in the previous administration and will be doing so with this administration as well.
I will be meeting with Mr. Kantor, the new U.S. trade representative, on Monday. I will be taking the same message.

Madam Speaker, I want to address the same minister with a very precise question.
The statement from Statistics Canada this morning said that out of the 63,000 people that counted for the decline in the unemployment figures, 57,000 were people who had totally dropped out of the labour market because they have no hope. Is that the way we are going to solve the unemployment problem by having Canadians simply drop out of the labour market because they know they cannot get a job?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. friend from Winnipeg is twisting the facts.
We have never expressed any degree of satisfaction with the level of unemployment today. That is why theMinister of Finance has done the things he did in the last economic statement and in the budget of a year ago.
Oral Questions
What my hon. friend must realize is that since September we have seen 161,000 jobs created in Canada. Surely my hon. friend would say that is good news and stop going around looking for bad news like the little Bad Luck Schlepprock next to him.

This party is looking for good news. That is why it is asking when and if the present government will begin to take measures to provide good news for Canadians.
I come back to the fundamental question. We have an increase this week alone of 6,000 on the welfare rolls of Toronto. In my own city of Winnipeg there are over
30,000	people on the welfare rolls, a 200 per cent increase over a few years ago. These are people without hope.
I want to ask the Minister for International Trade while the Prime Minister is down in Washington today: Is he going to understand for the first time that what the Americans are doing is what the Canadians should be doing and that is putting money into the economy to get people back to work and to create hope?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member mentioned Ontario and he mentioned Manitoba in his question.
Let me tell the hon. member that in the month of January, employment grew in Manitoba by over one half of 1 per cent and 43,000 new jobs were created in Ontario.
For Heaven's sake, when will the Liberals accept some good news instead of standing up here and bad mouthing the results that are happening in this country today which are positive and are leading to a recovery in 1993?

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
This week when Premium Automotive Tanks of Port Hawkesbury in Cape Breton closed and the owners, like thieves in the night, brought in trucks in the middle of the night, loaded them up and took the equipment downsouth to New Hampshire, they did not just take away the equipment. They took away the workers' pride, dignity and livelihood.


Oral Questions
This company received a large amount of government grants totalling almost $2 million and there are still some outstanding funds to be repaid. What steps is the government taking to get the repayment of the $500,000 of taxpayers' money that is still owing? Has the government given financial aid to Spectra Steel, the purchaser of this company?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. friend has acknowledged that Spectra Steel which is a company from Longueuil, Quebec has acquired the plant and will operate the plant in Longueuil, Quebec according to an agreement between Premium and Spectra.
The position of the Government of Canada is that officials have not allowed the repayment of the debenture by Premium to the Government of Canada until they are absolutely sure of the particulars of this transaction. This is to make sure that any transaction we have done is in accordance with the agreement they had made with ACOA. Officials from both the Government of Canada as well as from the province are actively working on this at this point.

Madam Speaker, the company, as the minister points out, has been sold to Spectra Steel and really had a terrible record. Certainly, that has been acknowledged by everyone. The company lied to the workers. One week before closing it was doing training with the workers and praising them for their productivity. When I spoke to workers yesterday they had one message and one message only for Ottawa: "We do not want a handout, we want a job".
The mayors of Port Hawkesbuiy and the surrounding area have written to the government asking if it will do a full investigation into this situation given the implication of federal funding as well as the effect on jobs in the area. Is the government prepared to undertake a full investigation in Port Hawkesbuiy as requested by these elected officials?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we on this side deplore the way this whole thing has happened. The Prime Minister spoke of that, the minister responsible for the Atlantic Cana-daOpportunities Agency has spoken about that and I have spoken about it. We deplore what has been done and how it has been done. As far as an investigation is concerned, there are officials working on this matter right now.
Rather than looking for all the bad news she can find, surely when my hon. friend goes to Nova Scotia she could visit the Michelin Tire Company which makes 12 per cent of the tires in North America, or Purolator Courier. Has she ever visited that company in Moncton which opened a service centre last October? It employs 100 people now and 400 people will be employed there over the next three years.
Did she ever congratulate Canadians who are providing the successes behind the 11.9 per cent increase in exports, many of whom come from communities like Moncton and Port Hawkesbuiy right across this country?

Madam Speaker, the last thing I need is a lecture from this government on respecting the workers of this country. The workers have built this country and if the government respected them it would not have signed the trade deal and it would not be contemplating following through with NAFTA.
It is clear as we look at what happened in Port Hawkesbuiy that job requirements for companies are absolutely essential when funds are involved.
There is another issue related to that. Through the NAFTA agreement we will not have the ability as a government to put those kinds of conditions on foreign companies that wish to take over Canadian plants. Under Articles 1106, 1107 and 1109 of the NAFTA agreement the government would not have the freedom from government imposed performance requirements or the freedom to repatriate dividends or royalties.
How on the one hand can the minister of trade condemn poor practices by companies and on the other hand sell out Canadian workers by signing a NAFTA that does that same thing and encourages it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, no one is selling out Canadian workers. If she would look at the facts she would see that there has been an 11.9 per cent increase in exports to the United States last year compared to the year before. There has been close to an $18 billion increase in exports to the United States since the free trade agreement came into force. That is double the rate that the Japanese, the Germans or the United Kingdom have increased their exports to the United States. Surely my hon. friend should see some good news in this.


I would ask her one thing. When in the last four or five years has she ever celebrated success in this country by going to some of these companies and hearing how they have increased their exports to the United States and asking them what impact the free trade agreement has had in that increase in exports which is creating jobs in Canada?

Madam Speaker, I certainly do not believe it is time to uncork the champagne bottles yet. There are still 1.5 million Canadians unemployed.
What is of extreme concern is that the unemployment figures released today reveal an alarming trend. Unemployed Canadians are giving up hope and are dropping out of the labour force. While this government claims we are in an economic recovery, the unemployment rate today is higher than it was in January 1992.
When will the minister accept that the unemployment situation in Canada is in crisis? When will he restore hope for those Canadians who have lost their jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I find it interesting. The hon. member does not recognize that there were
161,000	new jobs created over the last eight or nine months. That is a good, positive trend. The unemployment rate is dropping. That is a very positive thing as well. The hon. member must understand that.
The hon. member gets up in the House week after week and talks about youth unemployment. Let us talk about youth unemployment which is still unacceptably high. We are not popping open any champagne bottles. We are not celebrating anything, but the trends are very positive.
Oral Questions
The youth unemployment rate fell by 0.6 per cent. This accounted for a large drop in the unemployment rate. I might say that since over-all employment peaked for the fourth quarter of 1990, youth employment is becoming positive again. That is a good sign and is something the hon. member wanted all along.

Madam Speaker, if the minister is going to talk to us about statistics then perhaps we can respond. Canada lost 500,000 jobs during this recession. So far we have recovered only
161,000,	a far ciy from the 500,000 new jobs the finance minister predicted would be created in 1992.
What measures is the minister going to take to have an impact on this so-called jobless economic recovery?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member was in the House when the Minister of Finance delivered his economic statement in December and his budget earlier in the year.
There are provisions in there to help the economy, although modest, because of the limitations we have with the economy in the shape it is and with the income that the government has. We have taken some very positive stands and the statistics are showing.
The hon. member will not accept the positive good news. Housing starts are up 7.7 per cent. Employment in the construction industry in January was up by 18,000 jobs. Take the good news and run with it so that Canadians will build confidence in their economy and it can go on to recovery in 1993. Do not go around with a little black cloud over your head all day.

Madam Speaker, the minister had better check his facts because his facts are wrong about youth.
The minister must be aware that the number of youths now employed in the labour force has fallen by 103,000 in the past year. In the past five months alone, 90,000 young people have left the labour force. They are losing their jobs.
What concrete action will the minister take to create jobs for these young people?


Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know where the hon. member is getting his figures but mine show that I have employment has risen 0.6 per cent. The unemployment rate fell six percentage points for youth in the month of January. The jobs are starting to be created and we saw 161,000 new jobs over the last eight months.
They are getting back into the labour force and the jobs are coming back. That is what recovery is all about. It is going to continue in 1993 and Canada is going to have the best recovery of the G-7 in 1993. We have the basics in place with low inflation and low interest rates. The jobs are coming back.
The hon. member should be pleased about that and should encourage people who do the hiring in this country to continue to grow and expand.

Madam Speaker, one month does not a statistic make. We have a mammoth youth dropout rate; 44,000 more in the past month alone and over half a million young Canadians who have never held a first job. That is a 48 per cent increase since before the recession.
When is this minister going to give these kids a break? It was not their fault that there was a recession. When is he going to come forward with some concrete steps to put them back to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance has come forward with concrete steps and the hon. member knows that. We are starting to see the results of that. For heaven's sake, I just mentioned that in January-
One month.

One month, but the unemployment rate is dropping. The hon. member is obviously not happy with that. I could hear them today if the unemployment rate had gone up. Oh, my God, it would have been wild around.
They cannot stand good news over there. One of the problems is that the nonsense being spouted by the opposition does not give confidence to a country. They should start talking positively because the trend is increased employment and the creation of jobs, and the hon. member should be happy about that.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade.
Some months ago I raised in this House with the minister the aggressive pursuit of Canadian investment by the benefits of reduced taxes and lower electricity rates in the state of Texas. At that time the minister admitted that there was no method under the free trade agreement by which he could stop the Americans from this kind of procedure, regretted it and said he would look into it.
Today I would like to bring to his attention an even more aggressive move by the Americans, after the free trade agreement, into Canada through recruiting Canadian investments.
Here is a letter sent to Mr. B. M. Done, president of the Reliance Foundry Company in Surrey, B. C. It says to come to Iowa: "No property taxes for three years. No corporate state income tax. Fifty per cent of your employees' wages for one year while on-the-job training. A 1 per cent rate for unemployment costs. A non-union business community in a right-to-work state" and workers compensation down to $2.62.
What action will he take to stop this kind of raiding of Canadian investment, many in the United States, under the free trade agreement that is giving away our jobs to the Americans?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the facts speak for themselves. Prior to the free trade agreement we had a net inflow of investment of about $3.5 billion. Since the free trade agreement came into force we have had a new inflow of over $5 billion. I believe the figure for the first nine months of last year was a net inflow of $5.1 billion for a nine-month period.
Those facts speak for themselves and I think are a good attestation to the benefits of the free trade agreement.

Madam Speaker, this government refuses to stand up for Canadians. We have lost tens of thousands of jobs to the Americans, and even the Toronto Blue Jays cannot hire a Cuban because of American regulations.

What is going on? Who is running this country? Is it the United States or Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:

We must find ways to do this with the resources we have now.
In December, we increased the amounts allocated to help people receiving unemployment insurance benefits get new training and get back into the labour market. We included $260 million to develop what I call an unemployment prevention program for these people, which helps them identify human resources requirements in certain sectors of the economy. All thesemeasures-a total of $3.8 billion-are commitments under programs financed by the Consolidated Revenue Fund and the unemployment insurance fund, to help these people get back into the labour market. I hope he is there now, but a few minutes ago when the Clerk read the order for resuming debate on the bill in question, he was not even here. So how can you expect us to co-operate when the government acts this way? It is customary for us to be notified, to give our critic enough time to get here and respond to the government.
