He said: Madam Speaker, I did not have a chance to get up on the point of order with regard to how this bill was called so quickly, without any consideration to the process that normally exists when there is going to be a change in the Orders of the Day.
I spent three and one-half years as whip for the New Democratic caucus and I know there are courtesies. Effort is made to make sure that the parties know what the legislation is so that the various critics and various government spokesmen are able to be here.
I find it very regrettable that the government, in its haste to make sure it gets this legislation through the House, has ignored those common courtesies.
I resent it as an individual but I also resent it for those other people whose time has been inconvenienced. They may have appointments with me and with others and now are in a situation where those appointments cannot be kept. It affects people from in town and from out of town as well. I find this regrettable.
I am suggesting in the motions before the House that clause 1 be deleted. Through the day I am going to move that all the clauses in the bill be amended or changed. It is important that we have a debate on this at the appropriate time. I do not think this is the appropriate time.
As well, there is another debate that has to occur, that is about what is happening with the postal service across this country.
I have been the critic in this area, among my other critic roles, for a number of years. I am always receiving complaints from small operators, from employees, from-communities right across this country about how mail
service is being ruined by this government and by Canada Post.
I have found it offensive the way Canada Post officials deny information to members of Parliament and to the parliamentary committee that is responsible for reviewing the estimates for Canada Post. I have accused the top executives of Canada Post of misleading the House of Commons, the Senate and of being evasive when it comes to providing information which the public deserves.
The government has allowed this to happen. The government has allowed Canada Post to break its word. The government has allowed Canada Post to destroy our postal system in this country. There are all sorts of examples that could be cited as to why this is happening.
Why does the government want to destroy Canada Post? Why does it want to make sure that the various communities across this country do not get the postal service they deserve? Why is it in the community in which I live outside of Ottawa, there is about a one-half mile stretch that does not receive rural postal service? The mail people come from one end of the road to one area. They come from the other end of the road to another area. There are about 10 to 15 houses in between that do not receive regular service. They have to go to a different community to get their mail. It is ridiculous.
Just before the Christmas break I revealed a leaked Canada Post document about how they were going to force various franchises to pay up front for stamps and the various articles they sell on behalf of Canada Post. That document stated they were going to tell only some MPs about what was going on. They were not going to give this information about what was happening in the ridings to all MPs.
This document also pointed out that as a result of this change in strategy a number of those small businesses that are carrying on service on behalf of the public, on behalf of Canada Post, were going to go bankrupt. The Canada Post document pointed that out.
There was no concern for small business. There was no concern for the communities involved. There was no concern for the people who have to go and get their mail. This is the problem. I know that my good friend from-Timmins-Chapleau is going to point out later in the debate that this is a serious problem.


We have hurt the handicapped. We have hurt the seniors. We have made it ridiculously hard for people to get their own mail and we are doing it for some ideological interest which Canadians cannot understand.
We are told that Canada Post often surveys these communities ahead of time and that 97 per cent of the people want this change. This is very interesting. You can go into these same communities, as I and others in this House have done. Half of the population comes out to a meeting demanding that the post office be kept open.
I really resent the way the government has tried to handicap the opposition on this debate. Therefore I move:
That the debate be now adjourned.

speechtext: I have listened very carefully to the hon. member for Churchill. The House at this time is debating a motion which stands in the name of the hon. member for Churchill. Henceforth the hon. member may not move that during debate on his own motion. The motion is not receivable.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened to some of the remarks of the hon. member for Churchill and none of them to my hearing pertained to the bill in question.
He went off talking about mail service, small towns, a whole lot of things that are not dealt with at all in this legislation. Perhaps we will cause those who are looking down on us and watching on TV to have a little less disrespect than they now have because of those kinds of antics.
Fundamentally, this bill provides the opportunity for the provision of employee stock savings plans for employees of the post office. The hon. member for Timmins-Chapleau said privatization. In fact if he reads the act he will see that his accusation is totally false. There is no privatization involved here.
Government Orders
Not yet.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Not yet he says. That is right. A new bill would have to be brought in to privatize. That is a new bill. It sounds very strange. Vote against this bill because a new bill might come in sometime in the future. I know the New Democrats are scared of the future, but they should not deny everything in the present because of fear of the future.
I thought this might interest him. I received a letter earlier this week with some information about the Swedish post office. The Swedish post office is no longer a monopoly as of January 1, 1993. Other companies are allowed to compete in terms of delivering first-class letters. On January 1, 1994 the Swedish post office is to be privatized. That is the law of Sweden, a country glorified by the New Democratic Party as the example the world should follow. So Sweden is privatizing its post office.
The member for Timmins-Chapleau shouts back there that we should not proceed with this bill because some time in the future some government might bring in a bill to privatize the post office and hence we should vote against this bill. The logic speaks for itself.
This bill does a very sensible thing. It provides for employee stock ownership. Is employee stock ownership a good idea? The fact of the matter is that some two-thirds of the companies on the Toronto Stock Exchange provide for this sort of thing.
The group GBB Buck Consultants did a survey of companies with these kinds of provisions of employee stock ownership programs. It said that 90 per cent of employers and 75 per cent of employees said the plans had a positive impact in their companies and over 90 per cent of surveyed employees took pride in owning company shares.
Canada Post in the last few years has gone from running a deficit of $300 million to $400 million a year, where its service was atrocious, where it was a drain on the taxpayer and the laughing stock of the users to running a surplus and is recognized by other post offices around the world as the most efficient post office in the world. That is a tremendous accomplishment.
This bill seeks to build on that because employees of Canada Post now do feel pride in their corporation. They do feel that it is doing a good job and they do want theopportunity to participate. It is not compulsory. They are not required to. They are simply given the opportunity to.


Government Orders
The idea of employee stock ownership programs is so revolutionary that the current Government of Ontario has said it intends to bring in a plan like this. The current Government of British Columbia says it intends to bring in a plan like this to promote employee ownership of enterprise.
I find it not surprising, but a little bit strange that the federal New Democratic Party says this is an outrageously avant-garde idea that must be opposed by all means possible. That really does not make common sense. This is simply in keeping with modem business practices. It has been a success when it has been tried. More and more companies are doing it. The majority of companies do it. Even socialist provincial governments are adopting legislation to facilitate it.
I would be nervous about it if all these NDP members like it.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member has a point. If the socialists are now starting to like it maybe we had better re-examine it.
I am sorry, I said the B.C. government was considering it. It did it in 1989. The Ontario act was tabled in 1991 and of course Manitoba proclaimed its act in March 1991. It is a modern idea in keeping with modem corporations. It is something we ought to proceed with. This bill simply makes it possible.
I repeat, the amount of the equity that would be offered to employees is 10 per cent. That does not represent privatization in anybody's concept. The other 90 per cent rests with the Crown. If in fact that was to be changed and the Crown was to sell its shares, a separate new bill would have to be brought before Parliament.
The hon. member from the New Democratic Party and anyone else who thinks private ownership is an outrageous concept that should be fought at all times could in fact have their fight at that point in time.
I ask them to put aside their partisan interest, look at what this bill does, recognize it as it allows the continuing progress of Canada Post as a useful thing to do. The employees who choose to participate can. Those who do not will not. Ninety per cent of employers have found itsuccessful when they have put it in place and 75 per cent of employees have found it very useful.
With that kind of experience, that kind of evidence that it is a useful thing to do we ought to adopt this bill and allow the post office to carry on making the progress it has been over the last few years.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly disagree with what the hon. minister stated a moment ago, that the motions moved in this Chamber were not relevant to the bill or the debate before the House.
The reason the motions moved are relevant and the reason the remarks of the chief Whip of the Liberal Party before this debate started are relevant is that the bill itself is not relevant to Canada Post. The minister states: "Oh, we are now going to give employees shares in the corporation". I wonder what kind of shares.
First of all, they cannot have any more than 10 per cent, according to clause 27.1(5). We notice that the shares held by the minister have the exclusive right to vote at meetings of the shareholders of the corporation. We also note in clause 27.3 that the employees' shares will be non-voting shares. The employees' shares will be of a different character, a different class.
Second class.

Just like the employees of the corporation now are considered to be second class by the government and by the corporation.
When the Liberals were in, what a service we had. When the Liberals were in, we had post offices. We had post offices in rural areas. We had mailboxes in the post offices. There was a Canadian flag over the post office. The post office was the community centre. That is what happened when the Liberals were in.
When the Liberals were in we did not have calls in our offices that mail had just disappeared. We did not have every medical school and law school in this country rewriting their requirements so that they do not say that applications have to be postmarked on a certain date. It says the application has to be received in that university. That has been an intentional change by our professional schools in this country.
It has been intentional since this government took over and since the service has so deteriorated in this country, where a firm is hired to gauge the amount of time it takes for a letter to go from point A to point B. Itthen brags about it but does not explain of course that the letter it is passing judgment on has to have the address perfectly in the centre of the envelope. It is no good to have it written by a mother who is writing to her son overseas somewhere or in another part of Canada in pencil or pen.


This debate is relevant. The bill is irrelevant. That is why our chief Whip a moment ago asked me to move a motion. Of course I am going to do it because I never disagree with the chief Whip. The motion is this.

That the debate be now adjourned.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate this afternoon.
We have to remember the backdrop against which we are addressing this important issue today. First of all, the government changed the House order eight or nine times in the last 18 hours or so, including probably 10 seconds before it commenced the deliberations today.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Withdraw my allegation. Well, if we must debate that then let us. Let us do that simply because yesterday the government was telling us it wanted to debate Bill C-93 and then it changed its mind to Bill C-98, then to Bill C-93 again. speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I am sure the minister opposite who used to be the minister of agriculture and is now the minister of energy knows all of this but let us move on to Bill C-73.
We are talking of the post office and it pleases me to no end to talk about the post office today. Particularly today, because yesterday Canadians discovered to their astonishment some of the Canada Post policies. Here is how it works roughly.
If you are an ordinary garden variety MP and the postmaster retires in your riding, your post office is closed, period. Now, if you are the member for Charlevoix, the Prime Minister, and the postmaster retires in your riding, there is a different rule. Here is how it works. When the postmaster retires Canada Post refers to that as a natural opportunity. I suppose getting old or dying is natural. That natural opportunity is seized upon by the Tories opposite to shut down the post offices right across rural Canada.
In rural communities the post office is the only building with the country's flag on it. That is the post office in many rural villages in Canada.
What did Canada Post do? First of all it removed the coat of arms from its insignia. Then it removed the Canadian flag from its insignia. Not content doing that, now it is removing the post office altogether and there is nothing left. No more federal presence in rural Canada, no more Canadian flag. It is gone.
The member opposite is telling me to be careful about Canada Post. I do not know if he is going to send Don Lander after me if I am not careful or perhaps some of his spin doctors who are having lunch across the street in the National Press building. Half a dozen of them are trying to instil a message in the press different from the truth that we all know, to put it kindly. Nevertheless here is the truth.

The village of Saint-Irenee, with a population of 363, lost its postmaster, but it kept its post office anyway on December 1, 1992. Some of these villages are in the riding of the member opposite, others are in the Prime Minister's riding, like Baie-Saint-Paul, with a population of 3,733. I will even admit that if my riding had a community of 3,733 people, it might have kept its post office. In any event, the post office in Baie-Saint-Paul stayed open. As the hon. member knows, the same thing happened in Forestville: the post office stayed open. Saint-Simeon has a population of 1,020, which is not a lot. The postmaster resigned on February 4, 1991. It had an acting postmaster until March 9, 1992 and another one was hired. The post office stayed open. Good for them.
But why does the same rule not apply to other Canadians living in rural areas? As the member opposite knows, Saint-Joseph-de-la-Rive has a population of 225 and 35 houses; the postmaster quit and a notice was issued to hire another. The new one has not even been hired, but the post office is still open and it has been announced that a new postmaster was being hired. As we know, Bradore Bay is a Group 1 post office, the smallest kind there is in Canada-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: It's in my riding.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I know that it is in the riding of the hon. member for Manicouagan.


The postmaster retired, Canada Post advertised the position within the Corporation and no one applied. No one. What did it do? It advertised it a second time throughout the system, in the same region that time, not just at the local post office. Once again, no one applied for the position. It tried twice to fill it.
In Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, in Stormont-Dun-das, in Avonmore, in the riding of my colleague, the member for Gatineau-La Lievre, what did it do? It closed the post office the first chance it got! It has tried twice to keep it open in Bradore Bay. What did it do? It has still not found anyone who wants that job. It announced it would close the post office and it is still open today. So much the better for the people of Bradore Bay! But why a different rule for the Prime Minister's neck of the woods than for the rest of Canada and other members from rural areas?

Yesterday the Minister of Labour replied in this House that his government did not interfere with the operations of Canada Post. Tell that to the Minister of the Environment who is sitting across the way. Ask him about Lennoxville. Is the post office not still there in Lennox-ville even though Canada Post announced that it was closing? The Minister of the Environment is in his seat. I do not hear a heckle. Ask the Minister of Public Works what happened in his riding. It is the same thing.
There has been plenty of interference in the operation of Canada Post. Some ministers, particularly the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of the Environment have convinced the postal authorities to change their minds.
The Minister of the Environment knows it only too well, very well. He knows of the representation. The constituent in question was phoning him and me minutes apart trying to convince both of us to do our best to keep the post office open. That is not necessarily wrong.
What is wrong is that yesterday the minister gave us an answer that was less than accurate, to use parliamentary language. He said that the government did not interfere and the government Whip replied to that moments ago precisely. The government does not. He just repeated it.
Government Orders
Yet, Madam Speaker, I have indicted to you twice that that was not the case.
I know all of my colleagues will want to talk about this because it is an important issue for all of us.

Madam Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I take the opportunity to speak on Bill C-73 this afternoon. I do not think there is anything I would rather do than debate this bill today.
The minister responsible for Canada Post got up a little while ago and made reference to the comments of the member for Churchill who happens to be the critic for the New Democratic Party for Canada Post. He said that he talked about everything except the bill.
I want to inform the House that anything we say about Canada Post and the changes that are taking place in Canada Post do refer to this bill. I will demonstrate in a moment what I mean by that. The minister went on to say to me as the member for Timmins-Chapleau that in Sweden they have moved to privatize their postal services and that we in the New Democratic Party are always quick to refer to Sweden when we make a comparison between the working conditions and the conditions that exist there as they compare to the conditions that exist in Canada.
I would simply like to say to the minister that if he wanted to follow all of the examples that Sweden put forward in terms of protecting their workers and the working relationship they have with their employers maybe we would want to look at this a little more favourably. Until he is ready to do that I do not think we are ready to support this bill.
This bill is the employees' share savings plan. Its intention is to tiy to instil a little more pride and a little more partnership between the employer and the employee.
Plans have been tried before where they gave watches and they gave gifts and clocks and pieces of jewellery and what-have-you to try to improve the relationship between the employee and the employer, Canada Post. It did not work. It failed completely because it seems certain people within Canada Post Corporation are content to create a little empire to rule over and act like little dictators. Until that problem is addressed, these little gimmicks are not going to work. They did not work before and this gimmick is not going to work this time.

Government Orders
If Canada Post wants a share savings plan to work between the employer and the employees, why is it that prior to the introduction of this plan, it was never discussed with the employees that Canada Post wants to participate? The employees were never consulted during two years of negotiations prior to the introduction of this bill. Why is that? Is it because it does not matter what the employees have to say? Is it because Canada Post wants to throw this at them and say take it or leave it?
The minister is quick to say it is voluntary. Employees do not have to participate if they do not want to. That is fine but what does it mean? It means that only those at the higher levels will want to participate. They are the ones who will benefit the most from this because they have the most to invest. They have the most opportunities to take part in this program.
For those employees who will perhaps want to participate we are going to see a situation even worse than what exists now in terms of spying on each other and watching what is going on, trying to cut measures in order to create higher dividends.
That is the name of the game and that is what this corporation is heading for. It is heading for more profits and it is asking the employees through an employees' share savings plan to loan money to Canada Post in order for them, and I quote the minister, "to improve service". Does it mean Canada Post is going to maintain employment? Does it mean it is going to create employment? No, it does not. It is going to improve service. We are going to ask the employees to participate in a plan to lend the employer money in order to buy mechanisms and technology machines to put them out of work.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It's called productivity.

Productivity? Give me a break. It is called putting people out of work. The hon. member knows it.
This plan will not improve the situation at Canada Post. It will not do anything to improve the conditions that employees at Canada Post have to face day after day.
In my riding there is a small rural post office in a little town called Foleyet. The postmistress cannot even take lunch. She cannot even take a coffee break. Why? Because Canada Post eliminated the person who used to come in and help her for 20 hours a week. Canada Post has told her to close the wicket, just close it down. Never mind the people who are waiting outside. Never mind if it is a rural post office and people come from miles around to get their mail. Just close the door. Ignore them, do away with the service.
That post office is still open. Do you know why? It is making money. It is showing a profit. Do you know why it is showing a profit? Because there is no bank in that town. There are no other means for people to access any kind of a financial institution and they are using this post office instead. That is why Canada Post cannot close this post office down.
There are hundreds of these post offices in the riding of the member for Churchill, the critic for Canada Post. He has numerous situations under the same conditions where if the corporation would only realize that with a little bit of co-operation, with a little bit of help, these post offices would not only create jobs but they would also create profits. Are members opposite listening? They create profits. That is something the government knows about. That is something it wants. Along with profits, it creates jobs. What is wrong with that? What is wrong with jobs and profits? You can have it both ways, just try a little bit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Move into the next century.

Give me a break. Zip it up. This member is astounding. If you want to speak, get up and speak.
The employee share savings plan will work if Canada Post has the co-operation of the employees. The employees have been left out. They have been left out of all of these negotiations and therefore they will not support it. They do not want it. All the unions that represent the workers at Canada Post Corporation have said they do not trust this corporation and this is a move toward privatization. The minister has said it is not a move toward privatization. If it is going to be privatized, it has to have legislation introduced.
Again today he said that he admires Sweden for privatizing their post office. In the past he has said that he would welcome privatization of the corporation at a future date. All it needs is legislation.


With this government anything is possible. It has such a large majority it can jam anything through. Is privatization out of the question for this government? Absolutely not. Is this the way we want to go in this country? Is this what this government wants? It wants to privatize and put all these people out of work.
We cannot take the approach of cleaning up the problems that exist in Canada Post because if we get into this kind of a mess with employee share savings plan it really does not do anything other than loan the government money to put their employees out of work.
Perhaps it would work if these were at least voting shares and if they would actually produce a dividend. In 1991 the corporation lost $128 million. How much dividend would the employees get? How much return would they get?
The government will retain 90 per cent of the shares. We have to assume that it is going to do that at this point simply because it is issuing 10 per cent. Obviously this must mean that there are 90 per cent left. What is the government going to do with them? Will these be sold to the private sector? We do not know. The government has complete control. It does not need legislation to sell those shares. It is not necessary. These are voting shares and it can do with them whatever it wants. If they vote and decide to sell them, they can do it.
This whole bill is a disaster. It does nothing to address the problems that exist at Canada Post. It does nothing to enhance the lives of the employees at Canada Post. It does nothing to enhance service. It only creates more problems and it is certainly something that Canada Post does not need.
Bill C-73 is as much a disaster as some of the conditions that exist at Canada Post Corporation and this bill has got to fail.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to Bill C-73 which proposes to make amendments to the Canada Post Corporation Act.
The operation of Canada Post and mail delivery service in general is a very large issue across this country. Since I have been an elected member I have heard nothing but complaints about what Canada Post is doing.
Government Orders
Certainly long before I was elected I heard similar complaints. In my own riding we have had the closure of several post offices which have been very controversial. My local constituents have had a lot of difficulty in accepting some of the changes which have been made.
As has been raised by others of my colleagues here, it is of more than passing interest how the Canada Post Corporation, which the government says operates at arm's length from the government, happens to go across ridings, such as mine of Northumberland, closing small rural post offices which have in the past, and those that remain today, provided a very important and valuable service to the rural constituents. I do not want to belittle the important service that has been provided by our postal service over the years in this country.
A country as large as ours has to put a very special emphasis on maintaining very high standards in all of its communications and certainly our post office services are very important.
It is puzzling how Canada Post Corporation, operating at arm's length from the government, closes post offices and reduces postal services in a constituency such as mine, yet the constituency of the Prime Minister just happens to be able to maintain its usual services. We do not have constituents complaining in his riding as they might in mine.
I have tried my best to defend the interests of the constituents in my riding. The staff at Canada Post have done their best from time to time, but we know they have orders as to what they are to do and what they are not to do. It seems very obvious that this corporation is becoming more and more a private enterprise with profit as its main motive, not service to constituents across this country.
Yesterday a few members of our caucus had the pleasure of speaking to the National Pensioners and Senior Citizen's Federation. We had a chance to discuss with them many of the issues that are of great concern to them across the country and certainly postal service was one of their major concerns.
Their position is as follows. I would like to excerpt and have on record what they have to say about our Canadian postal service. I think it is relevant to the bill that is before us today.


Government Orders
The National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation wants the government to reconsider its decision to close all rural post offices. It reminds the government that almost 30 per cent of the membership of their group lives in rural areas. The government decision to close rural post offices has had a negative impact on those seniors' lives.
The Alberta Council on Aging stated in its brief to the federal government in 1990 that "seniors we talk to tell us the new services are much less satisfactoiy that the ones we had before when we had a knowledgeable, helpful and friendly staff in a rural post office".
The United Seniors of Ontario, said: "The rural mail delivery is an excellent service which should neither be reduced nor abolished. The supermailboxes are for the most part inaccessible to many seniors and should never be allowed to replace rural mail delivery at the rural post office". I have to say that in Northumberland I have had several problems brought to my attention by seniors who have had a lot of difficulty accessing the superboxes that exist in their communities, not just in the rural areas but in the suburban areas of my riding as well.
According to Rural Dignity of Canada, over 3,000 of Canada's small towns have concentrations of seniors, over twice that of the national average. I have many small towns in my riding of Northumberland. One-third of all Canadians 65 years and older live in communities of less than 10,000. As many as one-third of those 65 years and older do not drive.
Certainly the latest problem that I have had in my riding has been in the community of Hope Township where a post office was closed because of the very fact that many of the seniors do not drive and have to rely on others to help them. It has been a burden for them.
There was an attempt to try and set that closure of a post office right, but it does cause a lot of concern and change in a community that is at times very difficult with long-term impacts.
National surveys by seniors' networks show postal service to be among the top five issues of concern to Canada's elderly population. I bring that to the attention of our government because certainly it ought to be very concerned about the needs and desires of our senior population. When this is one of the government's fivemost important priority issues, it should certainly be stopping to listen to them.
The impact on seniors has many aspects, one of them being higher risks of physical danger. Outdoor boxes are placed in unprotected roadside locations without proper lighting or regular snow removal and seniors are at higher risk of physical danger. They create a loss of independence for seniors. In rural areas public transportation is non-existent. I can say that is certainly the case in most of my rural constituency. The superboxes and retail postal outlets may be split into two locations.
Those seniors without transportation are now required to depend on others to send or receive their mail. There is a loss of social contact that arises out of the closure of so many of our rural post offices. This was a contact that was very important to our seniors and allowed them to know that there was somebody who on a regular daily basis was there to check up and to follow what was happening lest there be some illness or accident that had befallen a senior citizen.
There is also a loss of a support network and the general lack of communication not just between a postal courier and a constituent, but also a constituent and neighbour. Since this government has undertaken the measures it has in the past to make changes to the Canada Post Corporation, communication across this country has suffered greatly.
The proposals that come forward in Bill C-73 today appear to me to be just one further step toward the privatization of Canada Post. As that occurs we have problems of loss of employment, loss of service to seniors, as I have just outlined, and loss of service to citizens of all types.
Other members have raised the issue of just how students who are trying to make application to get into university are hampered by our failing Canada Post Corporation's services across this country.
This is a vast geographical nation. We cover a large, large territory and it is imperative that we try to increase and improve our postal service. However, with the new and improved technologies that we have in the world today and with which Canada in particular is blessed, we find that instead of improved service we are paying more today for less and less service. Any moves in that direction which are going to exacerbate an existing problem I cannot support.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I greatly appreciate the opportunity to participate in the debate this afternoon.
Bill C-73 concerns Canada Post Corporation and gives the opportunity to employees of the corporation to share participation in the company. As has been noted, the availability of share participation has been deemed by responsible surveys to be a productive mechanism in 90 per cent of the cases. Indeed, 75 per cent of employees who have participated in such plans have favoured them as well.
While there is no way of knowing the extent to which Canada Post employees would take up this particular opportunity, the freedom for them to take it up or to refuse it is always there. I believe that the issue that is before us requires a good deal of debate.
In order to give an opportunity for all members of the House to participate, since we have had some interruptions today, I would move pursuant to Standing Order 26(1):
That the House continue to sit beyond the normal hour of
adjournment for the purpose of continuing consideration of Bill
C-73, an act to amend the Canada Post Corporation Act.
And more than 15 members having risen:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Pursuant to Standing Order 26(2), the motion is deemed to have been withdrawn.

Madam Speaker, I am going to be splitting my time with my colleague so I have only five minutes, I believe.
I want to be on the record to make just a few points. Number one, I have always been a strong supporter of the postal system in this country. In fact, I remember being part of a study in 1982 when we discovered that the postal corporation, Canada Post, had an efficiency rating of close to 96 per cent.
In terms of efficiency, that is something that is unheard of. This was when we had post offices all over the country. This is something where philosophically I am on the other side of the spectrum from the government. I believe that the post office system of this country was a great instrument of federal presence.
Government Orders
I can remember the period of the referendum. The postal service in Quebec was a tremendous agent in helping to keep this country together. I think of rural Canada and the number of postal offices that were closed there in the last few years. It does not really contribute to galvanizing the will of this country in pulling it together. From a federal presence point of view, Madam Speaker, I say through you to the government that I am totally opposed to all of these post offices that it is closing. A lot of Canadians do not realize that these postal offices provide services beyond mail in rural Canada and even in urban centres. They have been access points for senior citizens in terms of getting their pension plans and other programs organized, and so it is wrong to be chopping up that federal presence across the country.
The other point is that it is not just rural Canada. In my riding there were two post offices which were running most efficiently in downtown Toronto and which were closed in the last six months. I received complaints from small businesses, people who run home-based businesses and use the post office box system as part of their business practice. The fact that we shut down these main post offices and turn them into franchise units where they do not have the facilities to provide the same level of service I think is wrong.
With regard to the relevance of this bill, I have absolutely no problem with the concept of equity participation for employees. This is a good thing. What I am really concerned about in this particular bill is that there is a non-voting share. There does not seem to be a code of shareholders' rights attached to this bill.
How do you value these shares? We all know that the postal service of this country is actually showing profits, not out of its operating system, but it has actually been liquidating assets in terms of land and buildings. I am sure in my riding where it has shut down the post office that the next step will be to basically sell the land or sell the building so it can get some quick cash to beef up the financial statement so it can ultimately turn it into a totally privatized operation.
In business, people have a system of earnings per share per quarter where the bottom line is all that business looks for. In government, we are in the business of servicing people. I think that the direction thegovem-ment is taking with this act is working against service to the public.


Government Orders

Madam Speaker, Bill C-73 which is an act to amend the Canada Post Corporation Act, has one great fallacy. It fails to address the service of Canada Post to Canadians. Of all the things that Bill C-73 purports to do in terms of giving the shares of Canada Post, or an opportunity of those shares to employees, the government seems to be missing the biggest need and that is to address the postal service to Canadians in both rural areas and in urban centres.
We have tried to document with this government that closing stations, putting up supermailboxes, doing away with door-to-door delivery and removing the presence of the Canadian flag at postal stations across the country is not furthering or enhancing the sense of Canadianism and the important role that Canada Post has played traditionally through the many years. Not to even mention that there seems to be one rule in the ridings of regular members of Parliament and a completely different rule in the riding of the Prime Minister where the Canada Post stations are not being closed when in fact stations of greater service and of greater importance elsewhere are being closed.
The other point that I certainly want to dwell on in the few minutes accorded me in this debate is the way that Canada Post and the government approach public input. A postal station in my riding of York West was closed just a few days ago, Postal Station Downsview C in the Jane-Finch community. Canada Post officials late last year approached me because they were thinking of redesignating that postal service delivery. They had come at it from the standpoint of: "We wish to let you know this is what we are thinking of doing". I objected to that because I thought within the equation of that decision there was no thought given to what the clientele might think of redesignating or closing that particular postal station.
I suggested to them that it would only be legitimate and proper to delay any decision until they heard from the users, the clientele, the public, the community that had used that station for many years. Canada Post agreed with that process.
Then early in the new year I received a call saying that the building in which the postal station was located was sold and therefore they had to expedite their decision without public consultation. That decision was negative-because the decision was to close Downsview Postal Station C.
When we talk about indifference, cynicism and Canadians not believing in their institutions and governments any more and use this one classic example, is there any wonder?
The users of Downsview Postal Station C had absolutely no input and not one word to say about a post office that their taxes sustained and supported. I do not believe that is the way we should conduct public business. Canada Post is a public service to Canadians. Therefore we are having a public meeting next Thursday after the decision has been made.
Obviously there is going to be unhappiness and concern. It could have been managed and should be managed differently, not only for my riding but for the entire country. They should take Canadians into their confidence and allow Canadians the partnership to build and to redesignate and compromise so that both the community and Canada Post win. They should not shut out the communities. They should not agitate communities. They should not incite community activism which obviously will be organized now because of how things were done.
It certainly left bitter feelings in the community surrounding Downsview Postal Station C. It is not only a question of the stations that have been closed in the rural communities of Canada where it has taken on additional importance, but also in urban centres like my own city of metropolitan Toronto.
A lot of Canadians are dissatisfied with the postal service they are getting. There is a great deal of dissatisfaction that the user, the public, has no say. This is what we should be addressing in legislation before the House and not missing the mark and only talking about shares to employees. Let us talk about how we can improve this service for the benefit of all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I will be splitting my time with the member for Vancouver East.
North Surrey has the largest postal sorting service outside the city of Vancouver. About 18 months ago the postal station was informed that it would be closed and consolidated with the city of Vancouver. The local councils objected. The GVRD objected. The mayor of Vancouver objected. It is the wrong location. The services should be located in the suburbs where the people are. Surrey has a much better transportation corridor than the city of Vancouver. It is against the officialcom-munity living plan of the GVRD to consolidate employment in the downtown core.


I met with senior people in the post office, including the vice-president for mail operations. About that time they found out that the Vancouver post office was structurally unsound. They realized that they could not consolidate safely into the city of Vancouver. I was informed that was off and they were now going to look for property in the Fraser Valley, probably in Surrey, to consolidate a postal sorting service. As recently as the last two or three months I have been informed that this was continuing and was even told about potential sites.
About a week ago a letter was delivered to my office by fax, addressed to me, not to the post office workers or to the unions. It was addressed to me. It was announced that the government was going to close the Surrey postal service as of May 31.
I would like to read one paragraph from this letter because I think it shows what is happening with this corporation. It says: "Any potential impact on employees will be dealt with in accordance with their respective collective agreement. Canada Post Corporation will consult fully with affected unions. No employees will lose employment as a result of the new network processing system although some will be accommodated in other locations".
The three-paragraph press release that went with it contained other interesting points, saying: "Canada Post is consulting with all affected bargaining unions to fully discuss this change. Canada Post will continue to update employees on a regular basis as more information becomes available".
This letter was faxed to my office at seven o'clock in the morning. At ten o'clock I phoned the local union to get its reaction and found out that Canada Post had not informed the employees and had not informed the union. I was put on the speaker phone and that is how 100 workers in Surrey found out that their jobs were gone.
Then it came back and said it wanted to work co-operatively with the union and the workers. It did not even have the courtesy to inform them. It sent a letter, not addressed to the union and a copy, but it sent a letter to the MP because the MP had been on its backside for a year and a half insisting that it treat employees fairly and
Government Orders
keep the services in Surrey. It felt it had to pacify me but it did not have any regard for its employees.
Later that morning I talked to the local manager who told me that the letter was inaccurate, that 20 people would lose their jobs. Out of the 100 employees, 20 of them would actually lose their jobs in spite of the fact that the letter to me said this was not so.
Here the corporation went ahead in spite of local governments, the GDRD, the city of Vancouver, all pointing out to it that downtown Vancouver was not the place to locate the service. The transportation corridors were more appropriate to airport, rail and road in Surrey.
Then it had the audacity to go in and say it wanted the co-operation of the employees and it did not even follow common courtesy, let alone personnel practices and it ended up with the member.
This is repeated over and over again and I am sure my colleague from Vancouver East will have other comments along the same line.

Madam Speaker, I oppose Bill C-73 because it is the first step in selling off Canada Post. This post office, which has been so undermined by this government and by the Canada Post Crown Corporation has been an essential public service since the beginning of Confederation. As other speakers have said, post offices were the heart of most communities.
Privatization is deeply resented by most Canadians. The bill is misleading to employees. It is an attempt to undermine collective bargaining. It will not give real power to workers who purchase shares. It will not promote labour-management peace but will increase hostilities.
It does nothing to improve or maintain effective postal services in Canadian communities, communities that have been decimated by this government's inhumane privatization policies and action.
In my constituency of Vancouver East, a multicultural multi-ethnic riding, Canada Post has closed every post office. I have received frequent complaints about the services in the small franchised units which they have been attempting to develop in small stores. The importance of skilled and informed postal workers providing services to the community rather than having untrained,


Government Orders
overworked, underpaid and often part-time clerks in stationery or drug stores is very apparent in my riding.
Vancouver East is home to large Chinese, Korean, Italian, Latin American and other international communities. A thorough knowledge of international postal systems is vital for the maintenance of family communications. Sometimes it can mean the very survival of family members in the country of origin.
Yet with this new system it is understandable that part-time clerks who are untrained and underpaid do not have the skills to communicate with people of different cultures and to understand foreign procedures. Many franchise unit staff members simply do not seem to know postal procedures. The result is that people are forced to chase their parcels across the city and the country. Seniors, parents with young children and physically disabled people find the services inaccessible and sometimes impossible to use.
It is outrageous that this government has allowed this devastating deterioration of essential public services. I
could go on and on, but in the time remaining I would like to move:
That the House do now adjourn.
